_comment: Debate modes are interchangeable PROTOCOLS. Each `phases` object maps a phase name to the per-turn instruction given to an agent when the engine is in that phase. R/debate_engine.R::select_phase() maps a round number to a phase name using this ladder: round 1 -> 'opening'; final round -> 'closing'; the round before the final -> 'revision' (if present) else 'reflection' (if present); all other rounds alternate 'response' and 'cross_examination'. Any phase the engine asks for but a mode omits falls back to 'response', then 'opening'. Add a mode by adding an object here -- no R changes.

debate_modes.name: Oxford
debate_modes.description: Two sides argue a motion; structured rebuttal.

phases.opening: State your side's position on the motion clearly, with your two strongest supporting arguments.
phases.response: Rebut the previous speaker's strongest point directly, then advance a new argument for your side.
phases.cross_examination: Ask one pointed question exposing a weakness in the opposing side, then answer the strongest question posed to you.
phases.revision: Concede any point the debate has genuinely won against you, and sharpen the argument you are most confident in.
phases.closing: Deliver a closing statement: summarize why your side should prevail on the balance of arguments.

debate_modes.name: Delphi
debate_modes.description: Independent first estimates, then iterative convergence. Round 1 is blind: nobody sees another participant before committing.

phases.opening: Give your independent estimate/position on the question, with brief justification. Do not reference other participants.
phases.response: Having seen the range of positions, state whether and why you are revising your own. Move toward or away from the group as the arguments warrant.
phases.reflection: Identify the remaining source of divergence in the group and what evidence would resolve it.
phases.closing: Give your final position and your confidence in it.

debate_modes.name: Courtroom
debate_modes.description: Prosecution, defense, and a weighing of evidence.

phases.opening: Present your opening argument as prosecution or defense of the proposition, previewing your evidence.
phases.response: Examine the evidence just presented: what does it prove, what does it not, and what is missing?
phases.cross_examination: Cross-examine the opposing argument: expose assumptions, gaps, and admissibility problems.
phases.closing: Deliver your closing argument to the finder of fact.

phases.opening: Present a clear, falsifiable hypothesis relevant to the topic, with the mechanism you propose.
phases.response: Critically review the most recent hypothesis: strengths, flaws, confounders, and missing controls.
phases.reflection: Assess the statistical/evidentiary basis of the round's claims and flag weak inference.
phases.closing: Synthesize: what is well-supported, what needs more study, and the strongest hypothesis standing.

phases.opening: State the claim under review and the criteria by which it should be judged.
phases.response: Review against the criteria: major concerns, minor concerns, and what would need to change to accept it.
phases.revision: Propose the specific revisions that would address the concerns raised.
phases.closing: Give a recommendation: accept, minor revision, major revision, or reject, with reasons.

phases.opening: Ask probing questions only. Do NOT propose answers yet -- surface the hidden assumptions in the topic.
phases.response: Ask a follow-up question that presses on the weakest assumption exposed so far.
phases.reflection: Name the assumptions the questioning has revealed and which now look untenable.
phases.closing: Now answer the strongest open questions, citing which question you are answering.

phases.opening: Give your expert perspective on the topic in your own domain's terms.
phases.response: Respond to a point another panelist made, agreeing or disagreeing with reasons.
phases.closing: Give your final takeaway for the audience.

phases.opening: Contribute your opening view on the topic.
phases.response: Build on or challenge the discussion so far, adding something new.

phases.opening: Voice your stakeholder group's central concern or hope regarding the topic.
phases.response: React to another stakeholder's concern: where do your interests align or conflict?
phases.closing: State what outcome would best serve the people you represent.

phases.opening: Advance a position on the topic that you will then have to defend against attack.
phases.response: Attack the strongest standing claim as hard as you honestly can, then defend your own.
phases.revision: Repair your position against the attacks that landed, or abandon it if it cannot be repaired.
phases.closing: State what survived the adversarial process.

debate_modes.name: Fishbowl
debate_modes.description: A few speak while others observe, then swap.

phases.opening: As an inner-circle speaker, open the discussion on the topic.
phases.response: Respond to the inner-circle exchange, advancing the conversation.
phases.reflection: As an observer stepping in, reflect on what the inner circle missed.

phases.opening: Contribute your must-have requirement for any acceptable outcome.
phases.response: Identify which requirements are compatible and where the real tensions lie.
phases.revision: Propose a synthesis that satisfies as many must-haves as possible.
phases.closing: State whether you can endorse the emerging synthesis and any reservation you hold.

debate_modes.name: Policy Hearing
debate_modes.description: Testimony and questioning on a proposal.

phases.opening: Give testimony on the proposal from your expertise: expected effects and tradeoffs.
phases.response: Question the previous testimony on feasibility, cost, or unintended consequences.
phases.revision: Recommend amendments that would improve the proposal.
phases.closing: State your final recommendation to the committee.

debate_modes.name: Six Thinking Hats
debate_modes.description: De Bono's parallel thinking: the WHOLE panel wears the same hat each round -- facts, then benefits, cautions, gut reaction, new ideas, and finally process. Unlike every other mode this is driven by the round, not by each agent's role, so it works best with agents that carry no strong stance. Run 6 rounds for one hat each.

phase_sequence.name: White hat -- facts
phase_sequence.instruction: EVERYONE wears the WHITE hat this round; set your usual stance aside entirely -- for this round you are not arguing a position. State only what is known: facts, figures, sources, and precisely where the information is missing. Distinguish verified fact from assumption from guess. Ask no rhetorical questions and draw no conclusions.

phase_sequence.name: Yellow hat -- benefits
phase_sequence.instruction: EVERYONE wears the YELLOW hat this round. Set your usual stance aside. Look only for value: what could go right, who gains, under what conditions the best case is realistic, and why an optimistic reading might be the correct one. Do not balance this with objections -- the Black hat round handles those.

phase_sequence.name: Black hat -- cautions
phase_sequence.instruction: EVERYONE wears the BLACK hat this round. Set your usual stance aside. Look only for what could fail: risks, weak assumptions, unintended consequences, who is harmed, and the conditions under which this goes badly. Be specific and material -- caution is not pessimism, so name the mechanism of failure, not a mood.

phase_sequence.name: Red hat -- intuition
phase_sequence.instruction: EVERYONE wears the RED hat this round. Set your usual stance aside -- this round alone, nobody is required to be rigorous, cite anything, or stay in character. State your gut reaction, hunch or unease in a few sentences and do NOT justify it: no evidence, no reasoning, no hedging. The point is to surface the feeling the analysis has been suppressing, so it is on the record where it can be examined.

phase_sequence.name: Green hat -- new ideas
phase_sequence.instruction: EVERYONE wears the GREEN hat this round. Set your usual stance aside, and set aside whether ideas are realistic. Generate alternatives, reframings and possibilities nobody has raised: a different way to pose the question, an option outside the choices assumed so far, a provocation worth exploring. Quantity and novelty over defensibility.

phase_sequence.name: Blue hat -- process and conclusion
phase_sequence.instruction: EVERYONE wears the BLUE hat this round. Step outside the content and review the thinking itself: which hat produced the most, which was thin, what the panel now actually knows versus assumes, and what remains unresolved. Close with the most defensible summary the six rounds support -- and say plainly if they do not support one.

phases.opening: State only what is known: facts, figures and where information is missing. No positions.
phases.response: Take the perspective this round calls for -- benefits, cautions, intuition or new ideas -- setting your usual stance aside.
phases.revision: Generate alternatives and reframings nobody has raised yet.
phases.closing: Review the thinking itself and give the most defensible summary the discussion supports.

debate_modes.name: Narrative Forge
debate_modes.description: Myth-engineering loop: human problem -> competing moral frames -> candidate myths -> adversarial critique -> revision -> human testing -> cultural mutation -> further revision. Best with the Narrative role set; run 8 rounds for the full loop (fewer rounds compress it, extra rounds deepen the later stages).

phase_sequence.name: Human problem
phase_sequence.instruction: Do not tell stories yet. Articulate the HUMAN PROBLEM beneath the topic: what pain, need, fear, or conflict a narrative would have to address, who feels it, and why existing stories fail them.

phase_sequence.name: Competing moral frames
phase_sequence.instruction: Advance ONE moral frame for the problem -- a view of what is at stake, who owes what to whom, and what a good resolution would honour -- and contrast it explicitly with a frame another participant has advanced or could advance. Do not write the myth yet.

phase_sequence.name: Candidate myths
phase_sequence.instruction: Produce or contribute to a CANDIDATE MYTH that embodies one of the moral frames on the table: characters, setting, central conflict, symbolic objects, and the arc's key beats. Per your role, either draft narrative or specify what the draft must contain.

phase_sequence.name: Adversarial critique
phase_sequence.instruction: Attack the candidate myths per your role: propaganda potential, extremist appropriation, out-group creation, glorified obedience or violence, appropriated traditions, psychological mechanisms that misfire, structural weaknesses. Name the specific passage or element you are attacking.

phase_sequence.name: Revision
phase_sequence.instruction: Revise the candidate myths against the critique: state which objections you accept and how the story changes, which you reject and why. The revision must be concrete -- changed characters, altered beats, new imagery -- not a promise to change.

phase_sequence.name: Human testing
phase_sequence.instruction: Simulate reception: pick two distinct audiences (age, culture, disposition) and narrate honestly how each hears the current myth -- what resonates, what misfires, what is misread, where attention drops. Ground each reaction in a specific emotional mechanism.

phase_sequence.name: Cultural mutation
phase_sequence.instruction: Project the myth's drift: how retellings would mutate it over years of transmission -- simplifications, appropriations, inversions, merchandising, schisms. Identify which mutations are benign, which are dangerous, and which parts of the story invite them.

phase_sequence.name: Further revision
phase_sequence.instruction: Deliver the hardened final candidate: revise the myth against the observed mutations and misreadings, state what was changed and why, and name plainly the risks and disagreements that remain unresolved.

phases.opening: Articulate the human problem beneath the topic that a narrative would have to address.
phases.response: Advance the myth-engineering work per your role: frames, candidate narrative, critique, or revision.
phases.revision: Revise the candidate myths against the strongest critique raised so far.
phases.closing: Deliver the final candidate myth, with remaining risks and disagreements stated plainly.

debate_modes.name: Adversarial Scrutiny
debate_modes.description: Five-role protocol (Proposer / Challenger / Steelman / Source Auditor; the consensus engine acts as Synthesiser). Independent openings, structured challenge, fairness-tested critique, source audit.

phases.opening: Without reference to any other participant, state your independent opening per your role: your position or plan of attack/audit, the two strongest grounds for it, and the evidence you rely on.
phases.response: Perform your role on the debate so far: strengthen the case (Proposer); attack the weakest inferential step and state what alternative reading of the same evidence would overturn it (Challenger); test whether each standing objection engages the argument's strongest form (Steelman); report what the cited sources actually establish, claim by claim (Source Auditor).
phases.cross_examination: Name the single specific claim on which you and another participant are furthest apart. Ask them one pointed question about it, state explicitly what evidence would change your own view, and say whether that evidence exists.
phases.revision: Concede any point that genuine argument or audited evidence has won against you; restate your position with those revisions incorporated, and flag what remains unresolved.
phases.closing: State your final position: which of your claims survived scrutiny, which you modified or abandoned, and what remains genuinely uncertain. Do not introduce new arguments.
